content: Band 3 anion transport protein, also referred to as anion exchanger 1 (AE1) or solute carrier family 4 member 1 (SLC4A1), is a protein encoded by the SLC4A1 gene in humans. This protein is a highly conserved transport protein that facilitates the exchange of chloride ions (Cl−) with bicarbonate ions (HCO3−) across plasma membranes. Other functionally similar members of the AE clade include AE2 and AE3. Band 3 is located on the basolateral surface of α-intercalated cells in the collecting ducts of the nephron, which are the primary acid-secreting cells in the kidney. These cells produce hydrogen ions (H+) and bicarbonate ions (HCO3−) from carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) through a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. The hydrogen ions are actively transported into the collecting duct tubule by the vacuolar H+ ATPase, an apical proton pump, which excretes acid into the urine. On the basolateral surface, the kidney-specific isoform of AE1 (kAE1) exchanges bicarbonate for chloride, effectively returning bicarbonate to the bloodstream. This process serves two critical functions: (1) electroneutral exchange of chloride and bicarbonate across the plasma membrane on a one-to-one basis, which is essential for CO2 uptake by red blood cells and its subsequent conversion into protons and bicarbonate ions (a reaction also catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase), and (2) prevention of membrane surface loss, which is unrelated to membrane skeleton assembly. Band 3 is widely distributed across vertebrates. In mammals, it is specifically found in two locations: (1) the erythrocyte (red blood cell) membrane and (2) the basolateral surface of α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct of the kidney. The erythrocyte and kidney forms of AE1 are distinct isoforms of the same protein. The erythrocyte isoform, known as eAE1, consists of 911 amino acids and constitutes up to 25% of the red blood cell membrane surface. Each red blood cell contains approximately one million copies of eAE1. The kidney isoform, kAE1, is 65 amino acids shorter than eAE1 and is localized to the basolateral membrane of α-intercalated cells in the cortical collecting duct of the kidney. Mutations in the kidney-specific AE1 isoform (kAE1) can lead to distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, a condition characterized by the inability to acidify urine even when the blood is excessively acidic. Mutations in the erythroid AE1 isoform (eAE1) that affect its extracellular domains can alter an individual's blood group, as Band 3 determines the Diego blood group. More significantly, eAE1 mutations are responsible for 15–25% of cases of hereditary spherocytosis, a disorder associated with progressive loss of red blood cell membrane. Additionally, eAE1 mutations are implicated in hereditary stomatocytosis and Southeast Asian ovalocytosis. Band 3 has been shown to interact with carbonic anhydrase isoforms CA2 and CA4. The discovery of AE1 occurred through sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) of erythrocyte membranes. The prominent third band observed on the electrophoresis gel corresponded to AE1, which was subsequently named Band 3.
